title: What a program is
lesson:
A computer does exactly what it's told, one instruction at a time, very fast. It never guesses what you meant. A **program** is a list of those instructions written in a language both you and the computer can read. Python is one of the easiest to read, which is why it's a good first language, and it's also used for real work: AI, science, websites, robots, automation.

When you run a Python file, a program called the **interpreter** reads your file from the top, line by line, and does each instruction. If a line makes no sense to it, it stops and shows an **error** with the line number. Errors aren't failure: they're the computer telling you exactly where it got confused. Every programmer reads errors all day.

The first instruction most people learn is `print`, which shows text on the screen:

```
print("Hello")
```

The text goes inside quotes (that makes it a **string**, a piece of text) and the quotes go inside round brackets. Forget a quote or a bracket and Python stops with a `SyntaxError`: grammar mistake.

How to run your code: save the file, then press **check** (Ctrl+Alt+K in VSCodium) to have Archie run it against the tests, or run it yourself in a terminal with `python ex1_hello.py`.

example.code:
print("Hello, world!")
print("I am learning Python.")
print(2 + 3)
notes: Line 1 shows the text between the quotes.
Line 2 runs after line 1: programs run top to bottom.
Line 3 has no quotes, so Python works out 2 + 3 and prints 5.

exercises.title: Say hello
exercises.prompt: Make the program print exactly: Hello, Archie!
hints: Use print with the text in quotes.
print("Hello, Archie!") with the comma and the exclamation mark.

exercises.title: Three lines
exercises.prompt: Print three lines: your name on the first, the place you live on the second, and the number 2026 on the third (as a number, not in quotes).
exercises.starter:
# Line 1: your name
# Line 2: where you live
# Line 3: the number 2026 (no quotes)

tests.check:
src = CODE
assert src.count('print(') >= 3, 'Use three print lines.'
assert 'print(2026)' in src.replace(' ', ''), 'Print 2026 as a number: print(2026)'
tests.name: three prints, 2026 as a number

hints: Each print makes its own line.

exercises.title: Fix it (debugging drill)
exercises.prompt:
This program has three mistakes. Read each error Python gives you, fix that line, and run again until it prints:
Good morning
Today is a good day
10
exercises.starter:
print("Good morning)
print("Today is a good day"
Print(5 + 5)
hints: Run it and read the error: which line, and what does it say?
Line 1 is missing a closing quote, line 2 a closing bracket, and Python cares about capital letters: print, not Print.
exercises.solution:
print("Good morning")
print("Today is a good day")
print(5 + 5)

quiz.q: What does the Python interpreter do with your file?
choices: Guesses what you meant and fixes small mistakes
Reads it from the top and does each instruction in order
quiz.why: It runs top to bottom, exactly as written.

quiz.q: Python stops with SyntaxError. What does that usually mean?
choices: A grammar mistake, like a missing quote or bracket
quiz.why: SyntaxError means the line isn't valid Python, most often a missing quote, bracket or colon.

cards.a: A piece of text, written between quotes.

cards.q: Where does Python start running a file?
cards.a: At the top, one line at a time.

cards.q: What's the first thing to do with an error?
cards.a: Read it: it names the line and what confused Python.

bridge: Python needs no class or main: the file runs from the top. `print(...)` prints a line, and there are no semicolons or braces.
explain: Explain what a program is to someone who has never programmed, in your own words, with an example you make up (not one from the lesson).
